chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 12 of 21), sung at no named shrine: the poet confesses his bondage to women and courtesans who take a man's wealth, pictures old age, the funeral and Death's servants, traces a life from the womb to the pyre, and asks for the feet, for knowledge beyond the scriptures and sects, and for a place among the devotees; the praise turns on Krishna's boyhood, Siva's deeds, the freeing of the gods and Murugan as teacher of Siva.
structure_note: Death and the body: 1158 (the funeral), 1163 (womb to pyre), 1166 and 1167 (old age), 1169 (Death's servants), 1170 (the body and Yama's noose). Women: 1160, 1161, 1164, 1171. Knowledge and the feet: 1157 (the reality beyond scriptures and sects), 1159, 1162, 1165 (the five letters and Om), 1168 (the sea of births and the devotees' assembly).

1157.reading: The poet says the reality that the Vedas, the crores of Puranas, those infatuated with chariyai, kiriyai, sacrifice and yoga, and the debaters of rival sects chase and cannot know, is far off; he asks whether his mind will not one day melt in the Lord's light, join the compassionate devotees in the ocean of bliss, dance and rejoice, and sing without forgetting the jewelled lotus feet. The praise names Murugan as nephew of the cloud-dark Krishna who felled the marutha trees, sucked the demoness's breast, made the elephant scream and kicked the cart, and as the hero of the peacock, lord of Devayanai and the hunter girl and of crores of gods.
1157.nuance: The opening list sets the four Saiva paths (சரியை கிரியை ... யோக) beside the Vedas and the quarrelling sects (பரசமய பேத வாதிகள்) as things that run after the truth without reaching it; what is asked for instead is melting (உருகி), the company of devotees and song. மகோததி, great ocean, recurs in 1175 for the same bliss. The Krishna deeds (மருது, அலகை முலை, சகடு) are stock praise of the uncle.

1158.reading: The poet pictures his own funeral: kin, children and his sweet-spoken wife say it is over and he is cold, wail and beat their heads asking how this mistake happened, the fire-pot is carried, the drum sounds and the corpse is covered; he asks that at the hour his body is left Murugan give his two feet. The praise names the mountain daughter who rejoices while old ghouls dance to the drum, Siva in the tiger skin, the elephant-faced Ganapati who eats sugarcane and flattened rice as Murugan's elder brother, and the battle in which the night-walkers' clans fell.
1158.nuance: The funeral is told through the mourners' talk, which is hard to split in places (சலமிது சுத்தச் சலம், 'it is cold, quite cold'; மத்திப நடை): the reading of those lines is a guess. The plea is narrow: only at that moment (அப்பொழுது இருசரண் அருள்வாயே). The drum phrase தொக்குத் தொகுதொகு is rhythm, not words.

1159.reading: The poet says that while fire-priests and Soma-sacrificers fall prostrate at the pair of feet, he struggles with delusion and the senses, and his monkey mind is caught by women's sword-sharp eyes; he asks that darkness not cover it and that, in the dawn of attributeless knowledge, Murugan give him with love one of his feet. The praise has Siva, crowned with konrai, tulasi, datura, Ganga and the moon, and Vishnu with conch, discus and mace, beg Murugan to free the gods from prison, and names the vel he sent at the mountain.
1159.nuance: நிற்குண ஞானோதயம், the rising of knowledge without attributes, is the gift asked. The contrast between the ritualists (ஓமாதிகள், சோமாசிகள்) who already bow at the feet and the poet distracted by women is my reading of an opening whose syntax is not clear, especially திண்டிறல் தவ வாள்வீரரொடு இகலா.

1160.reading: The poet lists the arrows of women's eyes, sharper than carp, deadlier than poison, angrier than a deer, their speech of honey and syrup, their banyan-leaf bellies, hair, lips and smiles, and asks that he put desire for them far away and reach Murugan's feet with praise. The praise is of Siva, who kicked Death, burned Kama, begged at Kasi in Brahma's skull, rode the bull, held the poison, wore the elephant's hide and danced in the cremation fire with Uma at his side, and of Murugan his child, who sent the vel at the sea, Sura and the seven hills.
1160.nuance: The eye that wounds (விழிக் கணை) and speech like nectar are the usual weapons; the plea is simply to send desire far off (ஆசையினைத் தூரவிடுத்து). ஆதுலருக்கு at the end means the helpless or destitute: Murugan as lord of those without support.

1161.reading: The poet tells of cheating women who use love-powder, take the wealth in a man's hand by trickery, deck their breasts in silk and talk like parrots, and of his own madness in their bites and kisses; he asks for the wonder that cuts his attachment. The praise names the vel that pierced the demon army to battle drums, the vel that gives wealth to pure devotees who melt in grief, the lord of the green peacock, and Murugan who pointed out the meaning to Chokkar, Siva of Madurai.
1161.nuance: சொக்குப்பொடி is a love-drug and கைப்பொருளைக் கெத்தில் பற்றி is wealth seized by cunning, so these are the paid women. சொக்கர்க்கு அர்த்தத்தைச் சுட்டிய is the teaching of Siva again, with Siva named by his Madurai name. Lines 101 to 103 (திக்குக்கெட்டு ஒட்டுச் சிட்டென பட்டத்துற) are obscure.

1162.reading: The song opens with a string of names for Uma (giver of knowledge, cause of causes, the great Maya, Parvati) and names Murugan her son, guru of gurus, Valli's lord and the bridegroom of the heavenly deer-girl; the poet, calling himself a dog, asks to wear Murugan's feet on his head, to be rid of the fever of delusion, and to praise him rightly through learning. The praise names him as the one who came to Koodal and had the Jains who would not wear ash impaled so that the hunchbacked Pandya rose, as nephew of Rama who split Ravana, and as the lord beyond word and mind who destroys bonds.
1162.nuance: நீறு இடா அமணோர் ... கழுமீதினில் ஏறிட, கூனான மீனன் இடு ஏறிட, கூடலில் வருவோனே is the story of Sambandar at Madurai, here told of Murugan himself, with holy ash as the mark that divides the two faiths. சீர்பாத சேகரன், one who wears the feet as a crown, is what the poet asks to become. பாசவிநாசகன் names Murugan as the destroyer of the bonds.

1163.reading: The poet traces a life from the drop placed in the mother, growing like a pea into flesh, blood, limbs and nine openings, through ten months, birth and first steps, to falling under a woman's spell, walking bent with a stick, lying bedridden, Death coming first, the corpse lifted by weary sons and kin and burned on the pyre; he asks for the anklet feet so that this birth may end. The praise is a battle in which vultures and ghouls feast to drums, Indra and Brahma praise the vel that freed the gods, and Murugan is the son of Sankara who wears the moon, Ganga, konrai and serpents.
1163.nuance: The life runs without a pause from womb to woman to stick to pyre, so that the plea is against birth itself (செனனமிது தவிர), not only death. அந்தகன் is Death. சிங்கி, the woman's power over him, is literally a poison.

1164.reading: The poet describes women with shaking breasts, golden ornaments, anklets and a vina in hand, child-like speech and arrow eyes, who daily make love to a man and daily cheat him and seize his goods as debts; he asks for the feet so that, turning from their tricks and his own worthless ways, he may gain Sivam and hold to austerity. The praise is a battle sung in drum syllables in which the vel splits the demons and grinds the mountain to dust, and names Murugan the beautiful lord.
1164.nuance: கடன்பற்றிக் கொளும் மாதர், women who seize things as if collecting a debt, makes these the paid women. The goal is named in Saiva terms, சிவம் பெற்றுத் தவம் பற்ற. Most of the second half (தனந்தத்தத் தனந்தத்தத் ...) is rhythm.

1165.reading: The poet describes the Lord's form as made of the five letters, na the feet, ma the belly, si the chest, va the mouth, ya the crown, and of the syllables a and u of Om, the fullness that is knowledge within knowledge, and asks that he too recite it, make the lotus of his heart a temple and receive attentive knowledge. The praise appears to tell how Siva went to sea as a fisherman to seek and marry the fisher-girl, with Guha and the one cursed to be a makara in the story, and ends at the lord of light of the ajapa.
1165.nuance: நகரம் இரு பாதமாகி ... வாய் வகரமாகி lays the letters of நமசிவய on the body, and அகர உகர ... ஓம் adds the pranava; இதய கமல ஆலயம் makes the heart the shrine. The fishing story is my identification from the net (வலை), the fisher folk (பரதர்), the girl of the waves and the makara curse, as in the Tiruvilaiyadal tale; the syntax of the second half and the word அசபை (ajapa, the unspoken mantra) are uncertain.

1166.reading: The poet pictures old age, grey hair, fallen teeth, dried skin, failing legs, dim eyes and the staff, the body a slipping lump of flesh, and the illusion of a life called 'ours' that only brings grief; he asks whether his mind, still bound to women's musk-scented hair and kohl-dark eyes, will not turn to singing Murugan's golden feet. The praise is a long portrait of Siva, who taught the three poets, keeps the green lady at his side, begged alms, swallowed the sea's poison, burned the three cities and wears snake, Ganga, moon and herbs, and whom Vishnu and Brahma worship daily; Murugan taught the good to that Hara.
1166.nuance: The force of the song is that the old body and the lust come in the same breath: the mind is still tied to women (மிடைபடு சித்தம்) when the teeth are gone. உரையொடு சொல் தெரிந்த மூவர்க்கும் ... போதித்து may point to the three Tevaram poets, and நகையாதே may mean 'without seeing through (laughing at) this illusion'; both are uncertain.

1167.reading: The poet pictures the straight back bent, the face wrinkled, the belly sagging, the stick, the dim eyes and wandering mind, the wife spitting at the sight, others scolding and life slipping away, and asks whether before that day he will do dharma that bears fruit with a glad, cool heart, humbly bow to Murugan and rejoice. The praise is the battle with old Sura, the vultures and ghouls in the blood, and Murugan who wore white kadamba and married the goddess of the kurinji hills.
1167.nuance: Unlike most death songs, the plea is not for Murugan to come at the hour but for the poet to act before it: பயன்கொள் தருமம் புரிந்து, doing fruitful dharma, beside worship. The wife who spits (மனையாள் கண்டு உமிழ்ந்து) is the harshest touch in the picture.

1168.reading: The poet cries jaya to the Death of the Nirutar, the vel praised by the gods and the son of the pure one, worshipping the feet night and day, and asks that Murugan end his weariness in the sea of births that rises like seven seas, set him in the assembly of his devotees, give him knowledge and take him as his own: when will that day come? The praise tells how, after Indra's long penance in the form of a bamboo, Siva sent Murugan to free the gods, and how he went with his host, overthrew the mountain and Sura, freed the gods and returned to Hara.
1168.nuance: உனது அடியார் வாழ் சபையின் ஏற்றி, lifting him into the assembly where the devotees live, is the goal beside the ending of births. வேணுவின் உருவமாய் ... தவசினால் may allude to Indra hiding as a bamboo at Venupuram (Sirkazhi); I offer that identification as a guess.

1169.reading: The poet pictures Death's messengers coming with a roar like the sea, piercing the body, crushing it like sugarcane in the mill and cutting it with daggers while people cry out, and the women of the house and the women he loved falling on him weeping; he asks Murugan to see this and come. The praise names the Goddess by many names, Nari, Suli, Ambai, Mahamayi, Neeli, the mountain daughter beside the Lord the Vedas praise, and Murugan her son, wearing kadamba, the child who cut Sura apart.
1169.nuance: ஏமதூதர், Yama's messengers, here torture the body (ஆலைமீதிலே கரும்பு எனவே) rather than simply bind it, and the plea is the familiar one, கண்டு வருவாயே. Most of the praise is of the Goddess, not of Murugan.

1170.reading: The poet says the body of water, bone and skin takes life when father and mother desire, grows as a child into the joys of youth and lust for women, and at the end the buffalo-rider comes and throws his noose; he asks whether the illusion by which this flesh perishes will not end. The praise names the vel against Sura, Siva wearing bones and Ganga with his peacock-like consort, Vishnu who swallowed the earth, played the flute and walked after the poets' song, and Murugan as the life of devotees who sing the truth of the Veda.
1170.nuance: மேதியோன், the buffalo-rider, is Yama, and பாசம் வீச is his noose. பாவலோர்கள் பாடல் கண்டு ஏகும் மால is the story of Vishnu following a poet, as in 14. சூது மொழிவோனே, 'who speaks சூது' to Siva and his consort, I cannot place: it may mean subtle or secret words.

1171.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in detail, the gem string snapped by nails, the drinking of lips, faltering speech, sounding bangles, the perfumed bed and the tight embrace, in which he gives his mind and knowledge over to women, and asks whether he will ever give one moment to worship. The praise names the vel, the peacock, the cock banner and the hunter girl as what the poets who compose flawless Tamil set at the centre of their verse, and Murugan as the guru who made bloom for the three-eyed father the meaning of the teaching that the quarrelling six sects cannot reach.
1171.nuance: சட்சமயிகள், the six sects, deluded and quarrelling, cannot grasp the உபதேசப் பொருள் that Murugan gave Siva: the teaching story is set against sectarian argument. The Tamil poets who 'write and teach' (எழுதிக் கற்பித்துத் திரிபவர்) of the vel and the peacock are a self-portrait of the poet's own craft.

links.note: Both hear the funeral drum and see the corpse covered. The Naladiyar counts the beats with detachment and ends 'the dying carry the dead'; 1158 is the dead man's own view of his mourners, and turns the scene into a plea for the feet at that hour.

Both tell a life in one breath from the embryo in the womb. 9 stops at youth, women and disease; 1163 goes on to the stick, the bed, Death and the pyre, and so asks not for grace but for an end to birth.

Both show an old man with failing speech or teeth and a staff whose eyes are still on desire. The Naladiyar says such a man has no way to safety; 1166 is the old man's own confession and still hopes his mind will turn to song.
Both put good deeds before the body fails: the Kural before the hiccup stops the tongue, 1167 before the day the wife spits and life slips away. 1167 joins dharma to bowing before Murugan.
Both name Vishnu as the god who followed after a poet's song (பாவலோர்கள் பாடல் கண்டு ஏகும் மால், வண்டமிழ் பயில்வோர் பின் திரிகின்றவன்): a repeated formula for the uncle.

Tirumular 1446 matches the four paths to four kinds of men and lets only the last, the siddhas, reach Siva-knowledge (சித்தர் சிவஞானஞ் சென்றெய்துவோர்). 1157 sets those infatuated with the first three (சரியை கிரியை மக யோக மோகிகள்) among those who chase the truth and cannot know it. The song keeps the ranking but adds a limit: a path held with infatuation (மோகம்) does not reach, and what it asks for instead is melting (உருகி) among devotees.

The Kural says that for those whose delusion is gone (மருள்நீங்கி) and whose sight is clear, darkness leaves (இருள்நீங்கி) and joy comes. 1159 asks that darkness not cover (இருள் மூடாவகை) a mind caught in delusion (மோகாதி) and the senses, and that knowledge rise like dawn (நிற்குண ஞானோதய). The song turns the Kural's statement into a plea, with delusion, darkness and clear knowledge in the same order.

The Kural asks whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ), since it has all three. 1160 also measures women's eyes against three things: it says they beat the carp (சேலை அடர்த்து), have more of poison (ஆலம் மிகுத்து) and are fiercer than the deer (உழையைச் சீறு). The Kural's lover wonders at the look; the song makes the same comparison into arrows (விழிக் கணை) and asks to put that desire far away (ஆசையினைத் தூரவிடுத்து).

Both name the love-drug among the paid women's tricks: 1161 opens with சொக்குப்பொடி and wealth taken by cunning (கைப்பொருளைக் கெத்தில் பற்றி), and 1183 has பொடிமாயம், a drug that burns the belly (உதரம் எரிதர மருத்திட்டு). 1161 asks for the wonder that cuts attachment (பற்றற); 1183 asks to be taken out of that union. Drugging, beyond robbery, is a detail the courtesan songs rarely give, and here two neighbouring songs share it.

1162 asks that the poet, calling himself a dog (நாயினன்), become one who wears the feet as a crown (சீர்பாத சேகரன்). 1175 gives the same title to Murugan himself, who wears the anklet feet of the hunter girl (கிராதை நூபுர ... பத்மபாத சேகர). Put together, they show the devotee's posture of wearing the feet given to the god in his love for Valli.

Tirumular's town wails, takes away the man's name and calls him a corpse (பேரினை நீக்கிப் பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), carries him to the burning ground, burns him and bathes and forgets. 1163 ends a whole life the same way: sons and kin, worn out, call it a corpse (பிணமெனவே), say 'lift it, lift it' (எடுமெடுமின்) and burn it on the pyre (சுடலைமிசை எரியினிட). Tirumular stops at the mourners' forgetting; the song uses the scene to ask that birth itself end (செனனமிது தவிர).

The Naladiyar's wife feels shy each time her husband embraces her and wonders how women who embrace many men for gain (பொருள்நசையால் பன்மார்பு சேர்ந்து) do it every day (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). 1164 describes those women from the cheated man's side: daily they make love (தினம் ... புணர்ந்திட்டு), daily they cheat and seize his goods as if collecting a debt (தினம் தெட்டிக் கடன்பற்றிக் கொளும் மாதர்). The wife cannot imagine that daily trade; the song says what it costs the man, and asks for the feet so that he may gain Sivam.

Both lay the five letters on the body: Tirumular puts ந at the feet, ம at the navel, சி and வ at the shoulders and ய as the light above. 1165 has ந the two feet (நகரம் இருபாதமாகி), ம the belly, சி the chest, வ the mouth and ய the crown, then adds the அ and உ of Om. The two schemes agree on the feet, belly and crown and differ over the shoulders and mouth, so the body-mantra was not fixed in a single form.

In Tirumular the women who once wanted the speaker like sugarcane juice now find him bitter kaanjiram fruit (கரும்பொத்துக் காஞ்சிரங் காயுமொத்தேனே). 1167's old man is seen by his wife, who spits (மனையாள் கண்டு உமிழ்ந்து), while others scold. In both, the women's turning away marks old age; Tirumular stops at the change, and the song asks to do fruitful dharma (பயன்கொள் தருமம்) before that day.

The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்) and those who do not cannot. 1168 pictures births rising like the seven seas (திரை ஏழே போல் எழு பிறவி மாக்கடல்) and asks Murugan to end his weariness in it, give him his feet to wear (உனது தாளே சூடி) and lift him into the assembly of devotees. The song keeps the Kural's sea and feet and adds the devotees' company (அடியார் வாழ் சபை) as the place reached.

Tirumular says the true guru kept away the band of Death's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்) and ended the sorrow of birth. 1169 shows those messengers (ஏமதூதர்) at work, crushing the body like sugarcane in the mill (ஆலைமீதிலே கரும்பு எனவே) while the women of the house weep, and asks Murugan to see it and come (கண்டு வருவாயே). What Tirumular states as done, the song asks for at the very hour.

Tirumular says the Lord who made birth for joy shut it in the bond of sorrow, fastening skin and flesh to bone (என்பிற் கொளுவி ... தோல் தசை) until it runs to its end. 1170 builds the body from water, bone and skin (நீரும் என்பு தோலினாலும்), born of the parents' desire, running through youth and lust until Yama throws his noose (பாசம் வீச), and asks whether this illusion (மாயம்) will end. Tirumular gives the binding to the Lord's concealment, while the song gives it to the parents' desire and ends it with Yama.

Tirumular says the six sects are like six roads to one great city, and those who argue 'this is good, that is bad' are dogs barking at a hill. 1171 says the quarrelling six sects (கலகச் செற்றச் சட்சமயிகள்) cannot state or grasp (புகலற்குப் பற்றற்கு அரியது) the teaching Murugan gave Siva. Both blame the quarrel, not the sects as such; the song adds that the teaching itself lies beyond the arguers.

source_issues: Throughout: the source splits உ from the following letters with a space (உ ரையாடி, உ ததி, உ றைந்த), apparently a font conversion fault.
Song 1163: corrupt character in சிறைவை஢ட (line 163, probably சிறைவீட, 'free from prison'); unflagged slip அரவங்ளுந் (line 166) for அரவங்களும்.
Song 1167: corrupt character in ருத஧முழ்க (line 244, probably குருதி முழ்க, 'sinking in blood').
Song 1168: corrupt character in லு஡டே (line 259, probably ஊடே, 'through').
Song 1169: corrupt character in வீழ்வ஡ணது (line 286); the intended word is unclear.
Song 1170: corrupt character in உய஧ருறி (line 299, probably உயிருறி, 'life entering').
Song 1171: unflagged garble '....... ; த்ழுறல்' at line 319, probably for a word ending in ஊறல் (the lips' moisture).
